item.description:

Where voters stand on state ballot measures, from abortion to LGBTQ rights to guns
November 4, 20264:49 PM ET
By
Rachel Treisman
Voters weighed in on 146 statewide ballot measures across dozens of states.
Mario Tama/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Mario Tama/Getty Images
Tuesday's midterm elections were a huge sweep for Democrats, among other takeaways.
And across 39 states — plus Washington, D.C. and the Northern Mariana Islands — voters weighed in on 146 statewide ballot measures spanning issues from taxes to transgender rights to traffic cameras to data centers and AI.
Here's a look at some of those results.
Three states moved to preserve abortion access
The U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, leaving the legality and regulation of abortion up to each state. In subsequent elections, over a dozen states have put access to abortion on their ballots — and overwhelmingly moved to secure it.
This year, four states considered abortion measures. Three passed, while Idaho voted to preserve the state's abortion ban from 2022.

Elon Musk wasn't on Tuesday's ballot, but he stands to lose a lot from Democrats' sweeping midterm victories in the House and Senate. In no state was this more acutely felt than in Texas, home to the headquarters of Musk's companies and where he spent more than $200 million, according to federal filings, in a mission to sway the Senate race in the Republican candidate's favor.
With a Democratic majority in Congress, the billionaire, who controls Tesla and SpaceX, will likely face investigations into the billions of dollars of government contracts his companies have been awarded since President Trump returned to office and his role leading the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of Trump's second term.

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a midterm election night watch party at the Department at Hudson's on November 4 in Detroit, Michigan.
Salwan Georges/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
hide caption

Democrats coasted into victory late last night, taking control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate by considerable margins. Several states that are traditionally characterized as "deep red," including Texas, Kansas and Iowa, flipped towards Democrats in the Senate for the first time in decades. Democratic candidates also took a convincing majority in House races, despite competing in several states whose districts were redrawn to favor Republicans.
Across the country, Democratic gubernatorial candidates also burst ahead, winning races in GOP strongholds like Georgia, Ohio and Texas. Heading into 2027, Democrats will officially retake control of Congress and hold at least 28 governorships.

item.title: Herbert Blomstedt, conductor of great orchestras for seven decades, dies at 99
item.description:
Obituaries
Herbert Blomstedt, conductor of great orchestras for seven decades, dies at 99
November 4, 20263:11 PM ET
Tom Huizenga
Herbert Blomstedt conducts the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig in April 2026, at the age of 98.
Jan Woitas/picture alliance/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Jan Woitas/picture alliance/Getty Images
Herbert Blomstedt, an American-born, Swedish conductor whose remarkably long career saw him leading many of the world's major orchestras, including the San Francisco Symphony for 10 years, died on Wednesday at his home in Gothenburg, Sweden. He was 99.
His death was announced in a statement released by his management company, KünstlerSekretariat am Gasteig.
In a profession routinely flush with elderly practitioners, Blomstedt, year after year, retained his title as the world's oldest active conductor. He worked into his late 90s, conducting concerts this year, at the age of 98, with the Detroit Symphony and the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig, Germany.
"Retirement is not a question of age," Blomstedt told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. "It should be flexible. I just love the music so much that I just can't give up." And he didn't.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters Wednesday that the massive blue wave that brought Democrats control of the House and Senate signifies a "generational remake of the Senate map."
"These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want," the New York Democrat said outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington, D.C. "They entrusted us with the majority to do what they — the American people — want."
Democrats secured major gains in red states President Trump has previously carried, including Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Their victories include a history-making win in Kansas, which hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years.

item.description:

By

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., speaks with reporters alongside President Trump on Nov. 1, 2026, at Dubuque Regional Airport in Dubuque, Iowa.
Jacquelyn Martin/AP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Jacquelyn Martin/AP
Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app
After a bruising defeat for Republicans, House Speaker Mike Johnson does not plan to stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress, according to a source familiar with his plans who was not authorized to discuss them publicly.
The Louisiana Republican served two terms as speaker, elected after his predecessor, California Rep. Kevin McCarthy, was ousted in 2023.
Johnson's decision will open a role for the top House leadership position in the minority. Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections on Nov. 10.
Historically, the president's party loses seats in midterm elections. The blue wave soared past the expectations of many in Washington, flipping seats in traditionally red states that the president has won previously.
